title: Morgan Silver Dollar
subtitle: United States, 1878–1921 — one of the most reproduced silver dollars
key_facts: Composition: 90% silver, 10% copper
Official weight: 26.73g, diameter: 38.1mm
Struck at Philadelphia, New Orleans, San Francisco, Carson City and Denver mints
Common fakes are cast copies or struck from transfer dies made from a genuine coin
signs_real: Design details (Liberty's hair, eagle's feathers) are sharp and fully struck
Reeded edge is evenly spaced with no seam line
Rings with a clear, sustained tone when gently spun on a hard surface
Weight and diameter match the official U.S. Mint specification
signs_fake: Blurry or mushy design details, especially in the hair and feathers
A visible seam line running around the edge (sign of a cast copy)
A dull thud instead of a ring when spun or tapped
Noticeably lighter or heavier than the genuine coin, or slightly off in diameter
home_check_steps: Weigh the coin on a gram scale and compare to the official spec
Check the diameter with calipers
Look closely at the edge reeding under good light for a seam
Test with a magnet — genuine silver coins are not magnetic
care_tips: Store in a non-PVC coin flip or capsule
Handle only by the edges to avoid finger oils on the surface
Keep away from humidity to prevent toning damage
disclaimer: This guide is educational only. For high-value coins, always get a third-party grading service (e.g. PCGS or NGC) to confirm authenticity before buying or selling.

title: American Gold Eagle
subtitle: United States bullion coin — a common counterfeit target due to its gold content
key_facts: Composition: 91.67% gold (22 karat), alloyed with silver and copper for durability
Issued in 1 oz, 1/2 oz, 1/4 oz and 1/10 oz sizes since 1986
1 oz coin weighs 33.93g at a diameter of 32.7mm
Fakes are frequently gold-plated tungsten, which mimics gold's density closely
signs_real: Sharp, frosted design against a mirror-like or satin background depending on finish
Correct weight to the hundredth of a gram on a precision scale
Passes a magnet test — gold is not magnetic
Edge reeding is crisp and consistent
signs_fake: Design looks slightly soft or the fields look grainy
Weight is off even slightly — fake gold coins are often gold-plated tungsten or brass
Attracted to a strong magnet, or the coin's density feels wrong for its size
Edge reeding looks uneven or machine-stamped inconsistently
home_check_steps: Weigh on a precision scale accurate to 0.01g
Do a magnet test — gold and silver are not magnetic
Compare diameter and thickness to official specs
If in doubt, have it tested by a dealer with an XRF or ping tester
care_tips: Keep original mint packaging or a certified holder if available
Avoid touching the surface directly
Store in a secure, insured location
disclaimer: This guide is educational only. For high-value coins, always get a third-party grading service (e.g. PCGS or NGC) to confirm authenticity before buying or selling.

title: Walking Liberty Half Dollar
subtitle: United States, 1916–1947 — popular with counterfeiters for its silver content
key_facts: Composition: 90% silver, 10% copper
Official weight: 12.5g, diameter: 30.6mm
Designed by Adolph A. Weinman; later reused for the modern Silver Eagle reverse
Key dates like the 1916-D and 1921-D are the most frequently counterfeited
signs_real: Liberty's robe and the eagle's wing feathers are crisply struck
Correct silver weight and ring test tone
Mint mark placement matches known genuine examples for the date
Natural, even toning if aged
signs_fake: Soft, rounded details especially on Liberty's arm and the sun rays
Mint mark looks added on, misplaced, or oddly shaped
Unnaturally shiny or artificially toned surfaces
Fails the weight or ring test
home_check_steps: Compare the mint mark position and shape to a verified reference image
Weigh and measure the coin
Do a ring test on a hard surface
Check for file marks or seams along the edge
care_tips: Store flat in individual holders to avoid rim wear
Avoid cleaning — it destroys value even on genuine coins
Keep a written log of provenance if bought from a private seller
disclaimer: This guide is educational only. For high-value coins, always get a third-party grading service (e.g. PCGS or NGC) to confirm authenticity before buying or selling.

title: Ancient Roman Denarius
subtitle: Ancient Rome — frequently reproduced for the collector and tourist market
key_facts: Struck roughly 211 BC to the early 3rd century AD
Composition: silver, though purity dropped significantly over time
Hand-struck between two dies, so genuine coins are never perfectly round or centered
Museum and tourist-shop replicas are common and are often marked 'COPY' by law — check the edge for this stamp
signs_real: Irregular, hand-struck shape typical of ancient minting techniques
Natural wear patterns consistent with centuries of circulation or burial
Metal surface shows genuine aged patina, not painted-on color
Legends (inscriptions) match known genuine coin types for the emperor/period
signs_fake: Perfectly round, machine-made appearance uncharacteristic of ancient strikes
Artificial, uniform 'antiquing' that looks painted or chemically applied
Design doesn't match any documented genuine type — a red flag for a fantasy piece
Suspiciously light for its apparent silver content
home_check_steps: Compare the design and legend against a reference catalog (e.g. RIC)
Look at the strike under magnification for hand-struck irregularities
Check whether the patina looks layered/natural vs. flat and uniform
When possible, buy only from dealers who guarantee authenticity in writing
care_tips: Never clean an ancient coin — it can destroy both value and patina
Store in inert holders, away from PVC-based flips
Keep documentation of purchase and provenance
disclaimer: This guide is educational only. For high-value coins, always get a third-party grading service (e.g. PCGS or NGC) to confirm authenticity before buying or selling.

title: British Gold Sovereign

key_facts: Composition: 22 karat gold (91.67% pure), the rest copper for hardness
Official weight: 7.99g, diameter: 22.05mm
Minted continuously (with gaps) since 1817; also struck historically in Australia, India and South Africa
Widely faked because its small size and gold content make plating profitable
signs_real: Sharp St. George and the Dragon design on the reverse
Correct gold weight and diameter to the official spec
Passes a magnet test
Edge and rim details are clean and consistent
signs_fake: Design looks flat or slightly blurred compared to genuine references
Incorrect weight — often gold-plated base metal
Attracted to a magnet or has an unusual sound when dropped on a hard surface
Date/mint mark combination doesn't match any genuine year issued
home_check_steps: Weigh and measure against the official sovereign specification
Do a magnet test
Compare the date and mint mark to a genuine reference list
Check the edge for consistent, machine-even reeding
care_tips: Store in a capsule to prevent surface scratches
Avoid handling the face and reverse directly
Buy only from reputable, established bullion dealers
disclaimer: This guide is educational only. For high-value coins, always get a third-party grading service (e.g. PCGS or NGC) to confirm authenticity before buying or selling.

title: Chinese Silver Panda Coin
subtitle: China — one of the most counterfeited modern bullion coins
key_facts: Composition: .999 fine silver
The panda design changes every year, making a year/design mismatch an instant red flag
Size and weight specs have changed over the decades (e.g. 27g pre-2016, 30g from 2016 onward)
Counterfeits are produced at industrial scale, some good enough to fool a casual buyer
signs_real: Panda design details are sharp with visible fur texture
Correct weight and diameter for the given year's specification (sizes changed over the years)
Coin has the correct year-specific design, since the panda changes yearly
Surface has a genuine proof-like or matte finish depending on the issue
signs_fake: Panda design looks soft, flat, or slightly 'melted'
Wrong weight/diameter for the stated year
Design doesn't match the officially issued panda design for that year
Poor edge finishing or visible mold seams
home_check_steps: Look up the official design for that exact year and compare closely
Weigh and measure the coin
Check the edge for seams (sign of a cast fake)
Buy only from dealers who guarantee authenticity
care_tips: Store in original mint capsules when available
Keep away from humidity to prevent toning
Avoid excessive handling of the design surfaces
disclaimer: This guide is educational only. For high-value coins, always get a third-party grading service (e.g. PCGS or NGC) to confirm authenticity before buying or selling.

title: Mercury Dime
subtitle: United States, 1916–1945 — commonly altered to fake rare dates
key_facts: Composition: 90% silver, 10% copper
Official weight: 2.5g, diameter: 17.9mm
Officially named the Winged Liberty Head dime — 'Mercury' is a popular nickname
The 1916-D is the key date and the one most often faked by altering a common mint mark
signs_real: Full split bands visible on the reverse fasces for well-struck examples
Mint mark (if any) shows natural wear consistent with the coin's grade
Correct weight and silver content
Date and mint mark match known genuine combinations
signs_fake: Added or altered mint marks to simulate a rare date/mint combination
Mint mark looks slightly different in font or placement than genuine examples
Details look artificially sharpened or the surface shows tooling marks
Weight or diameter slightly off
home_check_steps: Examine the mint mark under magnification for tool marks or an odd font
Compare against a verified image of the same date/mint combination
Weigh the coin
When a date looks like a key rarity, get it authenticated before paying a premium
care_tips: Store individually to avoid contact marks
Avoid cleaning, which can remove evidence of alteration along with value
Get key dates certified by a grading service
disclaimer: This guide is educational only. For high-value coins, always get a third-party grading service (e.g. PCGS or NGC) to confirm authenticity before buying or selling.

title: Krugerrand
subtitle: South Africa — the world's most widely counterfeited gold bullion coin
key_facts: Composition: 22 karat gold (91.67% pure), alloyed with copper for a distinctive reddish tone
First minted in 1967; 1 oz version weighs 33.93g at 32.6mm diameter
Also issued in 1/2, 1/4 and 1/10 oz fractional sizes
Its long production run and popularity make it a top target for tungsten-core fakes
signs_real: Sharp springbok antelope design with fine coat texture
Correct gold weight (troy ounce fractions) and diameter
Passes a magnet test
Edge reeding is even and consistent
signs_fake: Springbok design looks soft or slightly distorted
Incorrect weight — often a gold-plated tungsten core, which mimics gold's density
Attracted to a magnet, or unusually dull sound when dropped on a hard surface
Poor quality edge reeding or visible casting seams
home_check_steps: Weigh on a precision scale — this catches most tungsten-core fakes
Do a magnet test
Compare diameter and thickness to official specs
Have a dealer perform an ultrasonic or XRF test for higher-value purchases
care_tips: Store in a sealed capsule or tamper-evident holder
Buy only from established, reputable bullion dealers
Keep purchase receipts and any certificates of authenticity
disclaimer: This guide is educational only. For high-value coins, always get a third-party grading service (e.g. PCGS or NGC) to confirm authenticity before buying or selling.

The 1933 date is illegal to own privately in most cases and any offered for sale should raise immediate suspicion

Passes a magnet test
Edge lettering (on the earlier variety) is even and correctly spaced

Edge lettering is uneven, misspelled, or missing on a variety that should have it
Surface shows file marks from a fake being altered to a rare date

Do a magnet test
Check the edge lettering spacing and font against verified references
Never buy an unauthenticated 1933 example — verify legal ownership history first
care_tips: Store in a certified holder from a major grading service
Avoid any cleaning or polishing
Insure high-value pieces and keep full provenance records

title: Spanish 8 Reales (Piece of Eight)
subtitle: Spanish Empire, 16th–19th century — heavily reproduced for the shipwreck and pirate-coin market
key_facts: Composition: silver, roughly .900–.930 fine depending on era and mint
Nicknamed 'pieces of eight' because it could be physically cut into eight bits for smaller change
Minted across Spain and its colonies (Mexico City, Potosí, Lima) with different mint marks
Genuine shipwreck-recovered examples usually have documented provenance and salvage certificates
signs_real: Irregular, hand-hammered or crudely milled shape typical of the era
Mint mark and assayer initials match documented combinations for the period
Wear and corrosion patterns are consistent with genuine age or seawater exposure
Comes with or matches documented provenance, especially for shipwreck coins
signs_fake: Overly uniform, machine-perfect shape inconsistent with hand-struck minting
Mint mark or assayer initials don't match any known genuine combination
Artificial 'sea-salvage' corrosion that looks applied rather than naturally formed
No provenance or documentation for a coin claimed to be shipwreck-recovered
home_check_steps: Compare mint marks and assayer initials to a reference catalog
Check whether wear/corrosion looks layered and natural vs. uniformly applied
Ask for and verify any salvage or provenance documentation
Weigh the coin against known genuine examples of the same type
care_tips: Avoid cleaning — original surfaces and encrustation can be part of the value
Store in an inert, acid-free holder
Keep all provenance and salvage paperwork with the coin
disclaimer: This guide is educational only. For high-value coins, always get a third-party grading service (e.g. PCGS or NGC) to confirm authenticity before buying or selling.
